# Assessment Tools vs. Closing BOD-25-01 Findings

## Why the order — remediate, then assess — is the difference between a compliance posture and a growing deviation list

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**[Download this whitepaper as DOCX](bod-25-01-close-before-assess.docx)** — a Word copy of
this page, regenerated on every site deploy. (Also available from the
**Other Formats** link in the page sidebar.)
:::
:::

### Executive summary

CISA [Binding Operational Directive 25-01](https://cyber.dhs.gov/bod/25-01/),
*Implementing Secure Practices for Cloud Services*, requires federal civilian
agencies to identify their Microsoft 365 tenants, implement the SCuBA Secure
Configuration Baselines against them, deploy CISA's ScubaGear assessment tool,
integrate with CISA's continuous-monitoring infrastructure, and **remediate
deviations** from the baselines. Agencies met the directive's early deadlines —
tenant identification by February 21, 2025, and ScubaGear deployment with
continuous reporting active by April 25, 2025 — and many now treat "ScubaGear
is running and reporting" as the compliance answer itself.

It is not. ScubaGear measures deviation from a baseline; it does not close any
of them. Neither does Microsoft's **Zero Trust Assessment** — the tool's actual
name, shipped as the `ZeroTrustAssessment` PowerShell module; “ZTTT” is this
series' internal shorthand and not a Microsoft designation — which many
agencies run alongside SCuBA to gauge broader Zero Trust maturity. Both tools
are, by design, **read-only diagnostic instruments** — the same category as a
thermometer. A thermometer that reports a fever every day for a year is not a
treatment plan, and an agency that runs ScubaGear on a schedule without an
architecture to close what it finds is reading the same thermometer on a loop.

This whitepaper makes the case, with the numbers behind it, for a specific
sequencing discipline: **close the architectural gap first, then assess** —
and keep assessing continuously afterward, because that continuous
reporting loop is itself a BOD-25-01 obligation, not an optional extra. Run in
the wrong order, ScubaGear and ZTTT each produce an accurate, growing list of
findings with no mechanism to act on them coherently. Run in the right order,
the same tools become exactly what the directive intends: confirmation that a
built architecture is holding, continuously, in evidence an assessor can trust.

### 1. What BOD-25-01 actually requires

BOD 25-01 is narrower and more concrete than "improve cloud security." Its
obligations, as issued:

| Obligation | What it requires | Status as of this writing |
|---|---|---|
| Tenant inventory | Report the tenant name and system-owning agency/component for every in-scope cloud tenant — M365 and, since the Google Workspace baselines gained BOD 25-01 Requirement indicators on 10 Jul 2026, Workspace too | First due Feb 21, 2025 — **not** one-time: agencies refresh the inventory in the first quarter of each year and keep it current through the fiscal year |
| Baseline implementation | Configure each tenant to the published SCuBA Secure Configuration Baselines (SCBs). **No longer M365-only:** CISA's Google Workspace baselines have carried BOD 25-01 Requirement indicators since 10 Jul 2026, so an agency with a Workspace tenant is in scope. All mandatory (“shall”) policies from the finalized baselines were due **20 Jun 2025** | Ongoing — baselines revise; agencies must track revisions |
| Tool deployment | Deploy CISA's assessor against every in-scope tenant — ScubaGear for M365, **ScubaGoggles** for Google Workspace (v1.0.0 GA 24 Jul 2026; v1.0.1, 28 Jul). ScubaConnect runs both: GearConnect for M365, GogglesConnect for Workspace | Due Apr 25, 2025 |
| Continuous reporting | Integrate assessor output (ScubaGear and/or ScubaGoggles) with CISA's continuous-monitoring infrastructure on an ongoing basis | Active since Apr 25, 2025 |
| **Remediation** | **Remediate deviations from the SCBs** | **Open-ended, ongoing obligation — this is the line agencies underweight** |

Four of these five rows are administrative or mechanical: report a tenant
name, install a PowerShell tool, wire up a feed. The fifth — remediation — is
architectural work, and it is the row the directive is actually *for*. A
ScubaGear report that faithfully lists forty deviations against the SCB every
week satisfies rows one through four. It does not satisfy row five, and row
five is not optional under the directive's own text.

### 2. What the assessors measure, and what they don't

ScubaGear and Microsoft's Zero Trust Assessment are both, in UIAO's adapter
taxonomy, `class: conformance` instruments — see the
[ScubaGear Integration whitepaper](scubagear-integration-whitepaper.qmd) for
the full canonical treatment. Neither writes to a tenant. Both read
configuration state and score it against a baseline (SCuBA's prescriptive
SHALL/SHOULD policies) or a maturity model (ZTTT's pillar-scored checks against
Microsoft's Zero Trust guidance). The
[Microsoft Zero Trust Assessment and CISA SCuBA whitepaper](zta-scuba-relationship.qmd)
covers the two tools' relationship in detail — they overlap almost entirely on
one surface (Entra identity) and otherwise cover different ground (SCuBA:
Exchange, Defender for Office 365, Teams, Power Platform; ZTTT: Intune devices,
Azure networking, Microsoft Purview data).

The distinction this whitepaper turns on is not *which* tool an agency should
run — the answer there is "both, for different questions" — it is what
*either* tool is structurally capable of doing once it runs. Neither can:

- **Design the Entra Conditional Access policy set, NTLM elimination
  sequence, and Arc Managed Identity chain** that moves a tenant's Zero Trust
  identity pillar from "Traditional" to "Advanced." ZTTT can score the gap; it
  cannot close it.
- **Design the DDI/IPAM grid** that makes DNSSEC and the network-layer
  controls SCuBA checks for actually enforceable across every environment the
  agency operates. ScubaGear can tell you DNSSEC is disabled; it cannot build
  the naming-and-addressing plane underneath it.
- **Resolve the GCC-Moderate boundary conflict** documented in
  [B.1.1](../orgcomp-series/boundary/B1-1-gcc-moderate-three-way-conflict.qmd),
  where TIC 3.0, Zero Trust, and FedRAMP 20x pull in genuinely different
  directions. Both assessors report symptoms of that conflict as separate
  findings; neither identifies the conflict as structural, because that is not
  what a conformance check does.

BOD 25-01's own "remediate deviations" clause presumes an agency *can*
remediate — that there is an architecture capable of absorbing the fix. Where
that architecture does not yet exist, "remediate" collapses into "re-run the
scan and file another POA&M line," which is compliance theater dressed as
continuous monitoring.

### 3. The coverage arithmetic — why "just run the assessor" undercounts the work

The Federal Organization Compliance (OrgComp) series quantifies this gap
against FedRAMP 20x's Key Security Indicators, in the section
["Why This Series — Not SCuBA, ZTTT, or Any Single-Vendor Assessment
Tool"](../orgcomp-series/Vol_0_Book_00_OrgComp_Executive_Summary.qmd) of Book
00. The arithmetic generalizes directly to the BOD-25-01 case:

**SCuBA-based rules attest 10 of 29 rules in the series' internal KSI
decomposition (KSI-001 through KSI-010)** — exactly the rules that reduce to
M365 tenant configuration state, which is exactly the surface ScubaGear
measures. **The other 19 exist as evaluable rules only because architecture
was built underneath them** — SBOM/VEX supply-chain evidence, privacy
data-flow mapping, training-effectiveness records, incident-response and
continuity architecture. No amount of running ScubaGear or the Zero Trust
Assessment more often produces evidence for those 19. They are not
configuration-drift findings; they are architecture that has not yet been
built.

The same shape holds for the BOD-25-01 remediation clause specifically: some
SCuBA deviations are one-line configuration flips an administrator can close
today. Others — legacy authentication still reachable because no phased
NTLM-elimination plan exists, or Conditional Access gaps that trace back to an
absent device-identity/NAC layer — are unclosable without the underlying
architecture. Treating both classes of finding identically, as "ScubaGear
says fix it," is how a remediation backlog becomes permanent instead of
shrinking.

::: {.callout-warning}
## ILLUSTRATIVE — replace before external release
For example, a `MS.AAD.1.1v1` ("Legacy authentication SHALL be blocked")
finding flagged in month `[N]` remained open for `[X]` months under
scan-only operation — repeated re-scans, no remediation owner — before
being closed in `[Y]` weeks once routed through the phased
remediate-then-assess sequence in §4.
:::

### 4. The correct sequence: architecture before assessment

OrgComp's modernization sequence — Understand, Design, Implement, Govern,
**Validate**, Authorize — deliberately places assessment tools at step five,
not step one:

| Phase | What happens | Where assessment tools fit |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Understand | Identify gaps and root causes against the target control set (including the SCuBA SCBs and Zero Trust pillars) | *Not yet run* — running an assessor here just produces an unowned findings list |
| 2 — Design | Select the architectural pattern that closes each gap with continuous evidence (DDI/PKI grid, NAC, Entra CBA, Conditional Access design) | *Not yet run* |
| 3 — Implement | Execute the runbooks, deploy the infrastructure, configure the integrations | *Not yet run* |
| 4 — Govern | Establish SCRM, POA&M, ISPP, and RACI structures to own what gets built | *Not yet run* |
| **5 — Validate** | Confirm the built architecture produces the compliance state it was designed to produce | **ScubaGear and the Zero Trust Assessment run here — as confirmation, not discovery** |
| 6 — Authorize | Submit KSI-ready, machine-readable evidence to FedRAMP 20x evaluators | Continuous ScubaGear/ZTTT evidence feeds the OSCAL bundle |

An agency that runs ScubaGear before phase 2 is, in the series' words,
"reading a thermometer before the treatment plan exists." The findings are
accurate. There is no framework yet to act on them coherently, so they
accumulate as a list of point fixes that never add up to a defensible,
integrated posture — and BOD-25-01's continuous-reporting feed just reports
that accumulation to CISA faithfully, on schedule, forever.

### 5. Closing findings first — what "architecture" concretely means here

For the specific surface BOD-25-01 governs (M365 / Entra), closing findings
before assessing means building, in this order, the layers a SCuBA deviation
or a ZTTT maturity gap actually depends on:

1. **Naming and addressing (DDI/PKI).** DNSSEC, certificate issuance, and
   several SCuBA network-adjacent checks are unenforceable without a
   functioning DDI/IPAM grid and certificate lifecycle underneath them.
2. **Device and workload identity (NAC, Entra CBA, managed identity).**
   The Conditional Access policy set SCuBA checks for, and the identity-pillar
   maturity ZTTT scores, both assume devices and workloads carry verifiable
   identity — which requires 802.1X/NAC on the network side and
   certificate-based auth or Arc managed identity on the workload side.
3. **Legacy-authentication elimination.** A phased NTLM/legacy-auth
   elimination sequence, not a single Conditional Access toggle, is what
   actually closes the SCuBA and ZTTT findings that reference legacy
   protocols — flipping the toggle without the elimination plan just breaks
   access for whatever still depends on the legacy path.
4. **Governance of exceptions.** Not every deviation is closable immediately.
   BOD-25-01 remediation does not mean zero deviations at all times; it means
   every open deviation is either being actively remediated or is a
   documented, dated, owned risk-acceptance — never a silent gap.

Only once these layers exist does "remediate deviations" become a bounded,
completable task instead of an open-ended chase.

### 6. Then assess — continuously, because the directive requires it

BOD-25-01's continuous-reporting obligation is not satisfied by re-running
ScubaGear manually before an audit. It requires exactly what a point-in-time
scan cannot provide on its own: a durable run-to-run record, aging of open
deviations against a remediation SLA, and a clean signal for "this deviation
is newly introduced" versus "this deviation is a known, governed exception."
UIAO's toolkit builds that layer directly on top of the assessors' output,
without reimplementing either assessor:

- **[ScubaDrift](../../../tools/scubadrift/README.md)** layers drift,
  exception-lifecycle, and continuous-monitoring gating on top of ScubaGear's
  pass/fail policy verdicts.
- **[ZTTTdrift](../../../tools/ztttdrift/README.md)** does the same for
  Zero Trust maturity-stage assessments (Microsoft ZTTT / CISA ZTMM-style
  self-assessments): it splits every below-target finding into
  **actionable new drift**, **lapsed acceptance**, or **governed exception**,
  flags retirable acceptances, computes run-to-run drift, and gates a
  continuous-monitoring pipeline — exiting non-zero only when something is
  genuinely unowned. Both tools are explicit about what they are not: neither
  is an assessor, a maturity model, or a remediator. They stand on the
  assessment tool's output; they do not replace it or guess at its export
  format.

This is the mechanism that turns BOD-25-01's "remediate deviations" and
"continuous reporting" clauses from a narrative claim into something a 3PAO
or CISA can independently verify: a deterministic, re-runnable disposition of
every open finding, dated, owned, and aging against an SLA.
[Vol VII Book 02](../orgcomp-series/Vol_VII_Book_02_OrgComp_M365_Control_Compliance_Automation.qmd)
of the OrgComp series documents the operating model that turns SCuBA baseline
drift specifically into typed remediation tasks with closure evidence — the
same pattern this whitepaper argues for at the directive level.

### 7. Honest limits

- **This is not a substitute for the directive's own deadlines.** BOD-25-01's
  tenant-inventory and tool-deployment deadlines already passed
  (Feb 21 and Apr 25, 2025, respectively). Nothing here changes those; the
  sequencing argument applies to how an agency spends its *ongoing*
  remediation effort, not to whether it deploys ScubaGear in the first place.
- **Some deviations genuinely are one-line fixes.** Not every SCuBA or ZTTT
  finding requires the architecture described in §5. The point is not "never
  fix anything until the architecture is done" — it is "don't mistake the
  scan for the fix," and to route findings to the right response (immediate
  config change vs. architectural work vs. governed exception) rather than
  treating all deviations as equally actionable.
- **ZTTT is not itself a BOD-25-01 requirement.** The directive names SCuBA
  and ScubaGear specifically; ZTTT is a Microsoft-authored maturity assessment
  many agencies run for broader Zero Trust posture. Conflating the two — or
  assuming ZTTT coverage substitutes for SCuBA's federal baseline, or vice
  versa — reintroduces the gap the
  [ZTA/SCuBA relationship whitepaper](zta-scuba-relationship.qmd) exists to
  close.
- **Coverage arithmetic (10 of 29) is the OrgComp series' internal KSI
  decomposition**, not a FedRAMP-published figure. It is a useful proxy for
  "how much of the target control set reduces to configuration state a
  conformance tool can see," not a claim about any specific agency's control
  catalogue, which will vary.

### 8. Conclusion

BOD-25-01 asks agencies to do two structurally different things: run an
assessor, and remediate what it finds. ScubaGear and Microsoft's Zero Trust
Assessment do the first job well — they are accurate, read-only, and
increasingly continuous. Neither does, or is designed to do, the second.
Confusing "the scan is running" with "the finding is closed" produces a
compliant-looking reporting feed sitting on top of an unclosed, growing
remediation backlog — technically satisfying rows one through four of the
directive while quietly failing row five.

The order that actually satisfies BOD-25-01 — architecture, then assessment,
then continuous re-assessment — is the same order OrgComp's six-phase
modernization sequence has argued for since Book 00: build the thing that
closes the gap, then measure that it's closed, then keep measuring. Run in
that order, ScubaGear and ZTTT stop being a list of open findings and become
what the directive actually intended them to be: continuous, independently
verifiable proof that a real architecture is holding.
